1.open: Think of a message you once received that really mattered, like a letter, a phone call or a text. Who was it from, and how did you hear it?
questions: The writer says God "spoke to our fathers through the prophets" on "many past occasions and in many different ways" (v. 1), but now "has spoken to us by His Son" (v. 2). Why might it matter that God's message comes in a person and not only in words?
Verse 3 says the Son is "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." If that is true, what does Jesus show you about what God is like?
The same verse says the Son is "upholding all things by His powerful word." How does it land with you to think of Jesus as holding things together, including the parts of life that feel shaky?

Verse 3 also says that "after He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high." Many readers take the sitting down to mean the work was finished. What does it mean to you that someone has already dealt with sin?
The writer spends most of the chapter comparing the Son to angels (vv. 4-14). Why do you think his first readers needed to hear that? What do people today tend to put alongside or above Jesus?

Verse 8 says, "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom." What does it say about a ruler that justice marks his kingdom? Where do you long for that kind of justice?

Verse 14 calls angels "ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation." What do you make of that picture of being cared for? If it feels strange or hard to believe, say so honestly.
Some days Jesus feels far away, and some days the claims in this chapter feel too big to take in. What would help you trust that God has really spoken, or what questions do you still carry?
1.life: Pick one of the Gospels and read a short story about Jesus each day this week. As you read, ask one question: what does this show me about what God is like?
1.prayer: Thank God for speaking clearly through his Son. Ask for eyes to see who Jesus is, and for trust where doubts or questions remain.
1.tip: The Old Testament quotations in verses 5 to 13 can feel like a maze, and the group may get stuck on them. Don't try to trace every psalm. Name the main point, that the Son is greater than every messenger, and offer to look at the details afterwards. Also say plainly that Christians differ on what the quotation in verse 5 has in view, then move on.

2.open: Think of a time you felt a little off course without noticing, like missing an exit or slowly losing touch with a friend. What was it, and how did you find out?
questions: The writer begins, "We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away" (v. 1). What does drifting look like in real life, and how can it happen without us choosing it?

Verse 3 asks, "how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?" The writer is not talking about people who attack the faith, but people who neglect it. What does that tell you about what he is worried about?
The writer quotes a psalm asking, "What is man that You are mindful of him?" (v. 6). When you think of how small we are, what do you make of God caring about us at all?
Verse 8 admits, "at present we do not see everything subject to him." Where do you look at the world, or your own life, and see things that are clearly not in order? What do you do with that?

In verse 9 we read, "we see Jesus," who "suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone." What stands out to you about the way the writer points us to Jesus rather than to a solution or an idea?
Verse 11 says Jesus "is not ashamed to call them brothers." What is it like to hear that Jesus is not embarrassed by you? Answer as honestly as you can, including if it is hard to believe.

Verse 15 speaks of people "held in slavery by their fear of death." What do people today fear that holds them back, whether death itself or something close to it? How might Jesus sharing our flesh and blood speak to that?

Verse 18 says, "Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted." When has it helped you to know that someone had been through what you were facing? What might it mean to bring your struggles to Jesus with that in mind?
2.life: Pick one habit that keeps you close to God, like a short daily reading, a weekly prayer with a friend, or showing up to group, and do it every day or week as planned. Notice what pulls you away from it, and tell God about that too.
2.prayer: Thank Jesus for sharing our flesh and blood and for understanding temptation and suffering from the inside. Ask him to help each person in the group stay close and not drift, and to help with whatever each one is facing this week.
2.tip: Verses 1 to 3 can sound like a threat, and some people will hear it that way. Help the group see that the writer is warning against drifting through neglect, not describing a God who is waiting to catch people out, and that the rest of the chapter is about Jesus drawing close to help. Also, the group may ask about Psalm 8. Say briefly that Christians differ on whether it is mainly about humanity that Jesus fulfills as the true human, or a direct prophecy about Jesus, and move on.

3.open: What is something you started with lots of energy but found hard to keep going over the long haul?
questions: The writer says to "set your focus on Jesus, the apostle and high priest" (v. 1). What does it look like for you to keep your focus on Jesus on an ordinary, busy day?

Jesus is compared to Moses, a man the first readers honored deeply. Moses was faithful "as a servant," but Christ is faithful "as the Son" (vv. 5, 6). Why might it matter that Jesus is more than a faithful servant?
Verse 6 says "we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast." What do you think it means to hold firmly, and what helps you do it?
The writer quotes the warning, "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts" (v. 7). What does a hardening heart look like in everyday life? How might someone not notice it happening?
The people Israel "saw My works" for forty years and still went astray (v. 9). Why can seeing good things from God still leave us doubting him?
Verse 13 says to "exhort one another daily" so that no one is "hardened by sin's deceitfulness." Who has encouraged you to keep going in your faith, and what did they do that helped?

Verse 19 says unbelief kept them from entering God's rest. Some Christians read the "if we hold firmly" lines as a warning that a believer could lose their place with God, and others read them as the sign that faith is real. However you read them, what do you do when your own trust feels thin?
If you are honest, where does trusting God feel hardest right now? What would a small step toward trust look like?
3.life: Pick one person in your group or church and send them a short message of encouragement this week, or ask how they are really doing. Verse 13 says to do this daily, so see if you can do it more than once.
3.prayer: Ask God to keep your hearts soft and listening today. Pray for anyone in the group who is tired, doubting or drifting, and for the courage to encourage one another.
3.tip: Verses 6 and 14 can sound like a threat to people who already worry about not being good enough. Name the disagreement plainly, then point the group to Jesus as the faithful one, and keep the tone one of encouragement. Make space for anxious or doubting people to speak honestly without being corrected.

4.open: When was the last time you felt truly rested, not just finished with a task? What made the difference?
questions: The writer says the Israelites heard good news, but it "was of no value to them" because they did not share the faith of those who heard it (v. 2). What do you think it means to hear a message and still not trust it?
Verse 4 points back to the seventh day, when "God rested from all His works." Why might the writer connect the rest we are promised with God's own rest, and not just a break from busyness?
Verse 7 says, "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts." What does a hardened heart look like in everyday life? How do you notice it in yourself?

Verse 9 says, "There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God." Christians read this in different ways: as peace with God now, as a future rest, or as both. How do you tend to picture this rest?
Verse 10 says that whoever enters God's rest "also rests from his own work." Where do you feel pressure to earn your place, with God or with other people?

Verse 12 says God's word "judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart," and verse 13 says everything is "uncovered and exposed" before God. How does that land with you: uncomfortable, comforting, or something else? Be as honest as you like.
Verse 15 says Jesus "was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin." How does it change the way you pray to know he understands weakness from the inside?
Verse 16 invites us to "approach the throne of grace with confidence." What makes it hard to come to God that way, and what might help?
4.life: This week, set aside one stretch of time, even twenty minutes, to stop working and simply be with God. When the urge to prove yourself or get something done shows up, notice it and let it go. Then pray verse 16 in your own words, asking for mercy and help with something real.
4.prayer: Thank God that Jesus understands our weakness and that we can come to the throne of grace. Ask for soft hearts that listen "Today," and for the kind of rest that comes from trusting him.
4.tip: Verses 12 and 13 can feel heavy, and some people may hear them as threat. Point the group to where the chapter ends: the same God who sees everything has given us a sympathetic high priest and an open invitation to mercy (vv. 14-16). Also, since Christians read "rest" differently, welcome each view without trying to settle it.

5.open: Who is someone you trust to give you honest advice, and what makes them easy to trust?
questions: The writer says a high priest "is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is subject to weakness" (v. 2). Why might someone who knows weakness firsthand be gentler with us?
Verse 4 says "No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God." Why do you think the writer stresses that Jesus did not appoint himself (v. 5)?
Verse 7 says Jesus offered "prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears." What does it do for you to picture Jesus praying like that?
Verse 8 says "Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered." What have you learned through a hard season that you could not have learned any other way?
Christians understand Jesus learning obedience and being "made perfect" (v. 9) in different ways, since most believe he never sinned. What do you take from these verses about his real humanity?
The writer says "You need milk, not solid food!" (v. 12). Where do you feel like you are still on milk in your faith, and where have you grown? Feel free to say if you feel stuck or unsure.
Verse 14 says the mature have "by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil." What practices help you grow, and what gets in the way?
5.life: Pick one small habit this week to help you grow, like reading a short passage each morning or asking a friend one honest question about faith. Tell someone in the group what you chose.
5.prayer: Thank Jesus that he understands weakness and listens to our cries. Ask God for a hunger to keep growing, and for patience with each other along the way.
5.tip: Verses 11 to 14 can sound like a scolding, and some people may hear it as a judgment on them. Point out that the writer is frustrated because he cares, and keep the tone of the discussion about growing together, not measuring who is mature.

6.open: What is something you had to wait a long time for, and what helped you keep going while you waited?
questions: The writer urges readers to "go on to maturity" instead of laying the same foundation again (v. 1). What does growing up in faith look like to you, and where do you feel stuck at the basics?
Verses 4 and 5 describe people who have been "enlightened," have "tasted the heavenly gift," and have "shared in the Holy Spirit." What do you think the writer is saying these people have received?
Verse 6 speaks of those who "have fallen away." Many readers think the first readers were tempted to give up on Jesus. What might make someone want to walk away from faith, then or now?

Christians differ on verses 4 to 6. Some think they describe real believers who could be lost, and others think they describe people who only tasted faith or serve as a warning to keep believers from that path. How do you hear this passage, and what questions does it leave you with?

In verses 7 and 8 the writer pictures two kinds of land, one that drinks in the rain and bears a useful crop, and one that grows "thorns and thistles." What might it look like in daily life to take in what God gives and let it bear fruit?

In verse 10 the writer says, "God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name." When have you felt that your effort for others went unnoticed, and what does this verse say to that?

Abraham waited patiently and then "obtained the promise" (v. 15). What is something you are still waiting on God for, and what makes the waiting hard? Be as honest as you like, including if you are not sure God will come through.
Verse 19 calls our hope "an anchor for the soul, firm and secure." What are the storms in your life right now, and what would it mean to hold on to Jesus in them?
6.life: Pick one thing you are waiting on or worried about this week. Each day, say verse 19 aloud, "We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure," and tell God plainly how the waiting feels.
6.prayer: Thank God that he keeps his promises and that Jesus has gone ahead of us as our high priest. Ask for steady hope for anyone in the group who is tired, doubting or tempted to give up.
6.tip: Verses 4 to 6 can frighten sincere people who fear they have lost their faith. Say early that Christians read these verses differently, don't try to settle it, and point the group to verses 9 to 12 and 17 to 20, where the writer is confident and offers assurance. Anyone worried about their own standing should hear that their concern itself is not the picture of someone who has walked away, and can be invited to talk with you afterwards.

7.open: Who is someone you could always count on to show up for you, no matter what?
questions: The writer says Melchizedek was "king of Salem" and "priest of God Most High" (v. 1), and that his name means "king of righteousness" and "king of peace" (v. 2). Why might it matter that one person is both king and priest?

Melchizedek appears in Genesis with no parents and no recorded death, and the writer says he is "like the Son of God" (v. 3). Why do you think the writer builds an argument on what the story leaves out?
The writer says "the lesser is blessed by the greater" (v. 7), and Abraham was the one blessed. What does that tell us about how this writer wants us to see Jesus compared with Israel's old priests?
Verse 11 asks why another priest was needed if the Levitical priesthood could bring "perfection." What do you think the old system could do, and what could it not do?
Verse 16 says Jesus became a priest "by the power of an indestructible life." What difference does it make that your priest cannot be replaced or run out of time?
Verse 19 speaks of "a better hope" by which "we draw near to God." When have you felt close to God, and when have you felt a distance? Be as honest as you like, including if it feels far right now.
Verse 25 says Jesus "always lives to intercede" for us. What is it like to picture someone speaking up for you right now?
Verse 27 says Jesus "sacrificed for sin once for all." How does that sit with you when you think about guilt you still carry?
7.life: Verse 25 says Jesus always lives to speak up for those who draw near to God. This week, set aside a few quiet minutes each day to come to God just as you are, without cleaning up your words first. Notice what changes when you remember he is already on your side.
7.prayer: Thank Jesus that he lives forever and is able to save completely. Ask God to help each person draw near with honesty, including anyone who feels far away tonight.
7.tip: The Melchizedek material in verses 1 to 10 can feel strange and tangled. Do not try to untangle every detail. Give the group the main point: Melchizedek's priesthood is higher than Levi's, and Jesus is a priest of that kind. Then move quickly to verses 24 to 27. Also, verse 12 on the change of law is read differently by Christians, some seeing the whole law as fulfilled in Jesus and others seeing only its priestly and sacrificial rules replaced. Name that in a sentence and keep going.

8.open: Think of a rule you followed as a kid that you never really understood. Did you ever come to see why it mattered?
questions: The writer says Jesus "sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven" (v. 1). What picture does that give you of Jesus, and of how close God is willing to be?
The old tabernacle is called "a copy and shadow of what is in heaven" (v. 5). A shadow points to something real. What is something in your life that points beyond itself to something bigger?
Jesus is called the one who mediates a covenant founded on "better promises" (v. 6). Why might people need someone to stand between them and God? How does that sit with you?
Verse 9 says the people "did not abide by My covenant." Where do you see that same struggle to keep promises, in the world or in yourself?

God says, "I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts" (v. 10). What is the difference between doing something because you were told to and doing it because you want to? Where have you felt both?

Verse 11 says "they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest." What does it mean that knowing God is not only for the experts? If knowing God personally feels hard or distant for you, what has that been like?
God promises, "I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more" (v. 12). What changes if you really believe that? Is there something you still carry as though it were not true?

Verse 13 calls the first covenant "obsolete and aging." Christians disagree about what that means for God's ongoing relationship with the Jewish people. How can your group talk about a question like that with humility and respect?
8.life: Pick one thing you do out of habit or duty, like praying, giving, or serving. This week, before you do it, tell God honestly how you feel about it and ask him to make it something you want to do.
8.prayer: Thank God that Jesus is our high priest, seated and close. Ask him to write his ways on your heart, and to help you rest in his promise to forgive.
8.tip: Priests, tabernacles and covenants can feel distant, so do not get lost in the details of verses 3 to 5. Keep returning to verses 10 to 12, the heart of the chapter, and handle verse 13 gently by saying plainly that Christians read it differently.

9.open: Have you ever had to follow a long set of rules or steps just to get into a place, like security checks, forms or a dress code? What was that like?
questions: The first part of the chapter describes the old tent with its two rooms and its curtain (vv. 2-3). If you had to explain to a friend why God's presence was kept behind a curtain, what would you say?
Verse 7 says only the high priest entered the second room, "only once a year, and never without blood." What does that tell us about how people in Israel understood God and their own need?
Verse 9 says the old gifts and sacrifices were "unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper." What is the difference between being outwardly in order and feeling inwardly clear?
Verse 14 says Christ's blood can "purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God." Notice that cleansing leads to serving. Why might the writer connect the two?

The writer says Christ "entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption" (v. 12). What do the words "once for all" mean to you, and where do they feel hard to believe?

Verse 22 says "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness." Many people find this idea of blood and sacrifice strange or even troubling. What questions or doubts does it raise for you? Be as honest as you like.
Verses 16 and 17 compare the covenant to a will, which only takes effect after a death. Christians read these verses in more than one way. What picture helps you understand why Jesus' death mattered?
Verse 28 says Christ will appear again "to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him." What does waiting for him look like in an ordinary week?
9.life: Think of one thing from your past that still weighs on your conscience. Once this week, tell God about it plainly, then read verse 14 aloud and thank him that Christ's offering was enough.
9.prayer: Thank God that through Christ we are not kept outside the curtain. Ask him to quiet any guilt that keeps us from coming close, and to help us serve him freely.
9.tip: The tent details in verses 1 to 5 and the will language in verses 16 and 17 can swallow the whole evening. Give each a minute, note that Christians read the will and heavenly tent images in different ways, then steer back to verses 12 and 14 and the question of a clear conscience.

10.open: What is something you keep meaning to get rid of or finish, but it stays on your list year after year?
questions: The writer says the old sacrifices were "only a shadow of the good things to come" (v. 1). What is the difference between a shadow and the real thing, and why might that matter here?
Verse 3 says those sacrifices were "an annual reminder of sins." When you have done something wrong, what actually helps the guilt go away, and what only keeps reminding you of it?
Jesus is pictured saying, "I have come to do Your will, O God" (v. 9). What does it tell you about God that his answer to sin was someone willingly coming, and not more offerings?

Priests stood and offered the same sacrifices again and again, but Jesus offered one sacrifice and "sat down" (vv. 11, 12). What might it mean that his work is finished? Where do you find it hard to rest in that?

Verse 16 promises, "I will put My laws in their hearts," and verse 17 says, "Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more." Which of those two is easier for you to believe, and which is harder?
Verse 22 says to draw near "with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith." If your faith feels small or full of questions right now, what would an honest approach to God look like for you?

Verses 24 and 25 talk about spurring one another on and not neglecting to meet. What has someone done that actually encouraged you to keep going, and what makes meeting together hard for people today?

Verses 26 to 31 are a stern warning, and Christians read them differently: some think true believers can never fall this way, and others see it as a real danger. However you read it, what do you hear in the writer's hope for his readers in verses 32 to 39, especially verse 39?
10.life: Pick one person in your group or church and encourage them this week with a call, a message or a visit. Tell them something specific you have seen God doing in their life.
10.prayer: Thank God that Jesus offered one sacrifice that is enough. Ask for the confidence to come near to him honestly, and for strength to keep going for anyone who is tired.
10.tip: Verses 26 to 31 can frighten sensitive people who worry they have sinned too much. Say gently that many readers take this as settled rejection of Christ, not everyday failure, and that Christians differ on the details. Then bring the group back to verses 19 to 23 and verse 39, where the writer is full of confidence in his readers.

11.open: Think of a time you set out on a trip, a move or a new job without knowing exactly what you would find. What was that like?
questions: The writer says faith is "the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see" (v. 1). How would you explain that in your own words to a friend who has never been to church?
Verse 3 says even believing the universe was formed at God's command takes faith, since no one watched it happen. What other things do we trust every day without having seen them for ourselves?
Abraham "obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going" (v. 8). What would make that hard for you, and what might have made it possible for him?
Verse 16 says these people were "longing for a better country, a heavenly one." Where do you feel a restlessness or longing that nothing here quite satisfies?
Verses 17 to 19 return to the story of Abraham and Isaac, which many readers find deeply troubling. What questions does it raise for you, and what does the writer say Abraham believed about God?
The list includes Rahab, described as "the prostitute Rahab" (v. 31), and others with messy stories. What does it tell you that these are the people held up as examples of faith?

Verses 33 to 35 describe people who shut the mouths of lions and people who were tortured, and all of them were "commended for their faith" (v. 39). Why do you think the writer puts both kinds of stories side by side?

Verse 39 says they "did not receive what was promised." If you are honestly struggling to trust God right now, or wondering whether he is there, what do you make of a chapter that admits the waiting is not over?
11.life: Pick one thing you are hoping for that you cannot see yet. Each day this week, tell God about it in a sentence or two, and do one small, practical thing that fits with trusting him for it.
11.prayer: Thank God for the people whose trust has gone before us, in the Bible and in your own life. Ask him to help each person in the group keep trusting him in what they cannot yet see, including those who are tired or doubting.
11.tip: Verses 33 to 38 can sting, because some of the faithful were rescued and others were not. Do not explain it away. Say plainly that the chapter holds both, and let people sit with that. Also, Christians differ on whether faith here is mainly inner trust or is bound up with obedience, so if it comes up, name it fairly and move on.

12.open: Have you ever run a race, a walk for charity or any long effort? What kept you going when you wanted to quit?
questions: The writer pictures "a great cloud of witnesses" around us (v. 1). Who has cheered you on in your faith, whether in person or through their example?
We are told to throw off "every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles" (v. 1). What is something that is not exactly wrong, but slows you down in following Jesus?
Jesus endured the cross "for the joy set before Him" (v. 2). What do you think that joy was, and how might it help you in a hard stretch?

Verse 6 says "the Lord disciplines the one He loves." Has anyone ever told you your suffering was God's discipline? How did that land, and how does the writer's picture of a father training a child sit with you?

Verse 11 says discipline is painful at the time, but "later on" it brings "a harvest of righteousness and peace." Can you think of a hard season that looks different now than it did then? If you can't yet, what makes that hard to say?

We are told to "strengthen your limp hands and weak knees" and to watch for bitterness taking root and spreading to others (vv. 12, 15). What can a group like ours do to help a weary person keep going without letting bitterness spread?

The writer says you have not come to a mountain "that can be touched" but to "the city of the living God" (vv. 18, 22). How does it change the way you think about approaching God to hear that Jesus makes that possible?
We are "receiving an unshakable kingdom," and also "our God is a consuming fire" (vv. 28, 29). How do gratitude and awe fit together for you? Which one comes more easily right now?
12.life: Pick one thing that is weighing you down or slowing you in your faith. This week, tell one trusted person about it and ask them to check in with you. Each day, take a minute to ask God for the strength to keep going.
12.prayer: Thank Jesus for going first and finishing the race. Ask God for endurance for anyone in the group who is tired, and for hearts full of gratitude and awe.
12.tip: Verses 5 to 11 can hurt if they are heard as 'God sent your pain to punish you.' Help the group see that the writer is talking about a loving father's training, not payback for every hardship. Also, the warnings about Esau and refusing God (vv. 16, 17, 25) worry some people. Say plainly that Christians read them differently, and avoid trying to settle it tonight. Keep coming back to Jesus as the one who runs ahead and finishes.

13.open: Think of a time someone welcomed you when you were new or a stranger. What did they do that made a difference?
questions: Verse 2 says some people "have entertained angels without knowing it." What makes it easier or harder for you to welcome someone you don't know?
Verse 3 asks us to remember those in prison and those mistreated "as if you were bound with them." What would it look like for our group to do that in a practical way?
Verse 5 says to "be content with what you have" and ties it to God's promise: "Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you." Why do you think the writer links money and God's presence?
Verse 7 says to "remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you" and to "imitate their faith." Who has shown you what trusting God looks like, and what did you see in them?
Verse 8 says, "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever." What changes in your life right now make that steady promise matter to you?
Verse 13 says, "let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore." What might it cost someone today to follow Jesus when it makes them feel like an outsider?
Verse 15 speaks of "a sacrifice of praise," and verse 16 adds doing good and sharing with others. Which of these two comes more naturally to you, and which is harder?
If you are honest, where do you find it hard to feel that God is near or helping you? What would you want to say about that?
13.life: Pick one concrete act from verses 1 to 3 or 16 and do it this week. Invite a stranger or newcomer for a meal, write to someone who is lonely or struggling, or share something you have with someone in need.
13.prayer: Thank God that Jesus is the same yesterday, today and forever. Ask him to make your group a place of welcome, and to help each person trust that he will not leave or forsake them.
13.tip: Verses 9 to 14 move quickly through Old Testament images like foods, altars and the camp, and scholars are unsure which food teachings are meant. Don't get stuck there. Give a one-line summary: Jesus died outside the city walls, and we are invited to follow him, trusting his grace. Then use the disagreement over verse 13 lightly: some read it as a call to break with temple worship, others as a call for any believer to accept being an outsider. Then move on to the practical questions.
